content: Bacterial pneumonia is an infection of the lungs caused by bacteria. The most common bacterial cause across all age groups, except for newborns, is Streptococcus pneumoniae. This gram-positive bacterium often resides in the throats of healthy individuals without causing disease. Another significant gram-positive pathogen responsible for pneumonia is Staphylococcus aureus. Gram-negative bacteria, while less frequently implicated, include Haemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Moraxella catarrhalis. These organisms often originate in the gastrointestinal tract and can enter the lungs when gastric contents, such as vomit, are aspirated. Atypical bacteria, such as Coxiella burnetii, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Legionella pneumophila, are so named because they tend to affect teenagers and young adults, cause milder symptoms, and require different antibiotics compared to typical bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae. Historically, bacterial pneumonia has been recognized as a severe infectious disease. It was a major cause of mortality during the 1918 Influenza Pandemic, earning the moniker captain of the men of death. Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most common causative agent, was first isolated in 1880 by Louis Pasteur and George Sternberg. The advent of modern antibiotics revolutionized treatment, but prior to their discovery, treatments like bloodletting were common, as described by William Osler in his 1892 textbook. Bacteria causing pneumonia can be inhaled from the environment or originate from the upper respiratory tract, where they migrate to the alveoli. Once in the lungs, the immune system responds by mobilizing white blood cells, particularly neutrophils, and releasing cytokines. While these mechanisms help eliminate the infection, they also produce systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, and fatigue. If bacteria enter the bloodstream, sepsis may develop, potentially affecting other organs like the brain, kidneys, and heart. Bacterial pneumonia can arise from various causes and is classified into typical and atypical categories. Typical bacteria often cause classic pneumonia, while atypical bacteria result in milder presentations, sometimes referred to as walking pneumonia. Patients with atypical pneumonia may appear relatively well but exhibit significant findings on chest X-rays. Pneumonia can also be categorized by age groups, such as neonates, children, adults, and the elderly, or by specific risk factors like alcoholism, aspiration risk, cystic fibrosis, intravenous drug use, immunocompromised states, or nosocomial (hospital-acquired) infections. Differentiating bacterial pneumonia from other pulmonary diseases is crucial. Laboratory tests, including chest X-rays, throat cultures, and bacterial sensitivity tests, aid in diagnosis. Conditions that may mimic pneumonia include bronchitis, bronchiolitis obliterans, empyema, lung abscesses, and pulmonary carcinomas. Other diseases to rule out include bacterial endocarditis, particularly in intravenous drug users, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and sinusitis. Pneumonia is prevalent worldwide, but mortality rates are disproportionately higher in lowand middle-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Seasonal variations influence case rates, with Streptococcus pneumoniae infections peaking in winter and declining in summer. Geographic factors are also significant, especially in cases of fungal pneumonia. Bacterial pneumonia can affect individuals of any age, gender, or race, though men are more commonly affected than women, and African Americans have higher prevalence rates compared to Caucasians. Socioeconomic status plays a role, with higher rates in lowto middle-income nations. Certain medications, such as proton pump inhibitors and ACE inhibitors, may increase susceptibility. Nosocomial pneumonia often develops within 48 hours of hospital admission, particularly in immunocompromised patients or those with prolonged hospital stays. Bacterial pneumonia is transmitted through oral secretions and progresses through stages of congestion, hepatization, and resolution. Symptoms typically include abrupt fever, chills, rigors, and cough. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets or contact with contaminated surfaces, with an incubation period of 1–3 days. Complications such as acute respiratory distress, pleural effusion, sepsis, and shock can arise, influencing recovery outcomes. Prognosis depends on factors like age and underlying conditions, with tools like the CURB-65 scale aiding in predicting disease severity and mortality risk. A detailed patient history is essential for identifying the underlying cause of pneumonia. Common symptoms include cough, fever, and pleuritic chest pain. Specific signs, such as diarrhea, hyponatremia, and anemia, may suggest particular pathogens. Physical examination findings vary based on disease severity, causative bacteria, and complications. Pulmonary findings and changes in vital signs are common, and complications like sepsis may lead to neurological symptoms such as confusion. Laboratory findings in bacterial pneumonia often include elevated white blood cell counts and inflammatory biomarkers like ESR and C-reactive protein. Anemia and thrombocytopenia may also be present. Arterial blood gases may reveal respiratory acidosis. Additional tests include electrolyte assessments, renal function tests, pulse oximetry, gram staining, and sputum cultures. Blood cultures and PCR tests provide definitive diagnoses and guide antibiotic selection. Chest X-rays remain the gold standard for diagnosing bacterial pneumonia, revealing patterns such as lobar or focal nonsegmental pneumonia, lobular or multifocal bronchopneumonia, and diffuse or interstitial (atypical) pneumonia. Radiological findings may take 6–12 weeks to resolve. CT scans, while not primary diagnostic tools, are useful in complex cases or when empirical antibiotic therapy fails. They help differentiate infectious from noninfectious pneumonia and provide detailed imaging of the affected areas. Other imaging modalities, such as ultrasonography, chest MRI, and lung biopsy, are less commonly used but can provide valuable information in specific cases. Ultrasonography is particularly useful for assessing pleural fluid, while lung biopsy is reserved for cases where the underlying cause remains unclear. Bronchoscopy may also aid in diagnosis, especially in non-immunocompromised or mechanically ventilated patients. Antibiotics are the cornerstone of treatment for bacterial pneumonia. The choice of antibiotic depends on the type of pneumonia, prevalent pathogens in the region, and the patient’s immune status and underlying health. In the UK, amoxicillin is the first-line therapy for community-acquired pneumonia, sometimes combined with clarithromycin. In North America, where atypical pneumonia is more common, macrolides like clarithromycin or azithromycin, or fluoroquinolones, are preferred. Local antibiotic resistance patterns should guide therapy. Hospitalized or immunocompromised patients often require intravenous antibiotics based on local guidelines. Primary prevention of bacterial pneumonia involves vaccination and managing underlying comorbidities. Pneumococcal vaccines, such as PCV13 and PPSV23, are recommended for specific age groups and high-risk individuals. Annual influenza vaccination is also advised. Strict control of blood glucose and blood pressure can reduce disease prevalence. Prophylactic antibiotics may benefit certain high-risk populations, such as asplenic children. Public education and identifying vulnerable individuals are key to reducing pneumonia risk. Secondary prevention focuses on preventing disease progression and complications. Measures include optimizing ventilator settings, reducing aspiration risk through head elevation and oral hygiene, and managing complications like acute respiratory distress, pleural effusion, and sepsis. The use of antibiotics and corticosteroids has proven cost-effective in treating community-acquired pneumonia, with significant savings in early treatment. Future therapies aim to address antibiotic resistance and emerging pathogens. Research is ongoing into host factors, such as genetic susceptibility and immune response, to develop targeted therapies. Genetic variants in genes like NGR1, PAK6, MATN1, and FER are being studied for their role in pneumonia susceptibility. Host-directed therapies focusing on immune resistance, repair mechanisms, and managing complications may offer promising advancements in pneumonia treatment.
